lesson.title: Components that break the pattern
lesson.orientation: Compare what a resistor does as the voltage rises with what a light-emitting diode does over the same range.

visualBrief.learningPurpose: Show a light-emitting diode in series with the resistor that sets its current.
facts: The diode and the resistor share one closed path.
The supply voltage is divided between the diode and the resistor.
The resistor value fixes the current in the branch.

objects.name: Series resistor
objects.description: The resistor that sets the current.

objects.name: Light-emitting diode
objects.description: The component with a forward voltage.

visualBrief.altTextDraft: A battery driving a series resistor and a light-emitting diode around one closed path, with the resistor labelled R and the diode labelled LED.
verificationChecks: The diode and the resistor are in the same single path.
The resistor value matches the supply voltage minus the forward voltage, divided by the current.

lesson.nextAction: Return to the course to review the whole set of circuit ideas you have worked through.

steps.headline: A component is ohmic if its resistance stays the same as the voltage changes.

lead.text: Then the current is proportional to the voltage: double one and the other doubles. Its graph of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin. A resistor is ohmic, so one resistance value describes it.

steps.headline: A diode is a one-way component.

lead.text: Current can pass through a diode in one direction only. The arrow in its circuit symbol points the way it can go. A light-emitting diode (LED) is a diode that gives out light.
Plot an LED's current against its voltage. A resistor gives a straight line. Think about what a one-way component might do instead.

reveal.text: Almost nothing flows until the voltage reaches the LED's forward voltage. Then the current climbs steeply. The LED is not ohmic.

lead.text: Use what you know about a diode's direction.

reveal.text: A diode passes current one way only. Reversed, it blocks, so the circuit carries almost nothing.

steps.headline: A red LED has a forward voltage of 2 V. It runs from a 9 V supply at 20 mA. Find the series resistor.

workedSteps.text: Past its forward voltage an LED's current climbs steeply, so something else must set the current. The LED keeps 2 V and the resistor takes the rest.
Divide by the current, 20 mA = 0.02 A.

steps.headline: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 5 V supply at 15 mA. Find the series resistor.

workedSteps.text: Find the voltage left for the resistor.
Divide the leftover voltage by the current, in ohms.

lead.text: Same job, new parts. The LED keeps its forward voltage and the resistor sets the current.

blocks.text: A resistor carries 0.02 A with 2 V across it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell an ohmic component from a diode, and choose the series resistor that sets an LED's current.

recap.keyIdea: An ohmic component has constant resistance. A diode does not: it passes current one way, and past its forward voltage its current climbs steeply, so a series resistor sets the current.

blocks.text: You found that 5 V, a 2 V LED and 15 mA need a 200 Ω resistor, and that doubling the voltage on a resistor doubles its current.

recap.nextHook: Review the whole course: which rule fits which circuit?

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode is connected the wrong way round in a low-voltage direct-current circuit. What happens?
hints: A diode conducts in one direction only.
Think about what the reversed connection does to the current in the branch.
Decide what the learner would observe.

acceptedIdeas: almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark.

choices.label: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
The diode lights with the same brightness as before
The current doubles because the path is shorter
The diode lights more brightly and cools down

questions.onCorrect: A diode passes current one way only, so a reversed LED stays dark.

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing a diode matters: it is a one-way component.
A shorter path isn't the issue. Think about which way a diode passes current.
A reversed diode can't conduct better. It is a one-way component.

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 5 V supply at 15 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The LED keeps its forward voltage. How much of the supply is left for the resistor?
Convert 15 mA to amperes.
Divide the leftover voltage by 0.015.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 5 V − 2 V = 3 V. With 15 mA = 0.015 A, R = 3 V / 0.015 A = 200 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 200 Ω. The resistor takes what the LED leaves and sets the current.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the whole supply voltage. The LED keeps its forward voltage.
Check the units. Convert milliamperes to amperes before dividing.

questions.prompt: Explain why a light-emitting diode is normally wired with a resistor in series with it.
hints: Think about how sharply the diode's current changes once its forward voltage is reached.
Ask what would set the current if the diode were the only component in the path.
State what the resistor does to the current in the branch.

rejectedIdeas: the resistor makes the diode brighter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Past its forward voltage the diode's current rises steeply for a very small voltage increase, so the diode cannot set its own working current. The series resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current in the branch.

questions.onCorrect: The LED's current climbs steeply past its forward voltage, so a series resistor takes the rest and sets the current.

questions.prompt: State what it means for a component to be ohmic, and give one example of a component that is not.
hints: Consider the shape of a graph of current against voltage.
An ohmic component gives a straight line through the origin.
Name a component whose graph is not a straight line.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An ohmic component keeps the current proportional to the voltage across it, so it has a constant resistance. A diode is not ohmic, because its current climbs steeply once the forward voltage is reached.

questions.onCorrect: Ohmic means current proportional to voltage, so the resistance is constant. A diode is not ohmic.

questions.prompt: A resistor carries 0.02 A with 2 V across it. What current does it carry with 4 V across it, in amperes?
hints: Use Ohm's law to find the resistance first.
2 V and 0.02 A give a resistance of 100 Ω.
Now divide 4 V by that resistance.
questions.onCorrect: 0.04 A. The resistance stays 100 Ω, so double the voltage gives double the current.

misconceptions.feedback: The current changes when the voltage does. Find the resistance, then use it at the new voltage.

questions.prompt: A resistor is ohmic. What does its graph of current against voltage look like?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: A straight line through the origin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straight line through the origin

choices.label: A straight line through the origin

questions.onCorrect: A straight line through the origin: constant resistance means current proportional to voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: A bend means the resistance changes with voltage. That is not an ohmic component.
A flat line would mean the current ignores the voltage.

questions.prompt: The arrow in a diode's circuit symbol points from left to right. Which way can current go through it?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?
questions.onCorrect: Left to right only: the arrow shows the one direction a diode passes.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow points the way the diode passes current, not the way it blocks.
A diode is a one-way component. It does not pass current both ways.

questions.prompt: The voltage across an LED rises slowly from 0 V. What does its current do?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply

choices.label: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
Rises in a straight line, like a resistor's

questions.onCorrect: Near zero, then a steep climb past the forward voltage: an LED does not follow a straight line.

misconceptions.feedback: A straight line is what a resistor does. An LED is different.
More voltage does not lower the current in a forward-biased LED.

questions.prompt: Why does the series resistor get the voltage the LED leaves over?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply

choices.label: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
The LED switches the resistor on

questions.onCorrect: Series voltage drops add to the supply, so the resistor takes what the LED does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The LED doesn't switch anything. Think about how voltage drops in series add up.
The resistor's voltage depends on the supply and the LED. It is not fixed.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery lights a blue LED with a forward voltage of 3 V at 10 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The LED keeps its forward voltage. How much of the supply is left?
Divide that leftover voltage by the current, in amperes.
10 mA is 0.01 A. Work out the leftover voltage divided by 0.01.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 9 V − 3 V = 6 V. R = 6 V ÷ 0.01 A = 600 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 600 Ω. Take off the forward voltage, then divide what's left by the current.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the whole 9 V. The LED keeps its forward voltage; the resistor gets the rest.
Check the units. The current is in milliamperes, so convert it to amperes first.

questions.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 12 V supply at 25 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: Subtract the LED's forward voltage from the supply.
Convert 25 mA to amperes.
Divide the leftover voltage by 0.025.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 12 V − 2 V = 10 V. R = 10 V ÷ 0.025 A = 400 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 400 Ω. The resistor takes the leftover voltage and sets the current.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the whole supply voltage. The LED keeps its forward voltage.
Check the units. Convert milliamperes to amperes before dividing.
